model.name: Alias / Same-as Mapping
model.purpose: Provide a reusable, format-neutral mixin for asserting that two identifiers, records, labels, representations or real-world entities stand in a declared equivalence, replacement or non-equivalence relation, carrying the asserting authority, the evidence basis and a confidence or strength declaration, so that federated identity equivalence can be exchanged without collapsing every link into an undifferentiated sameAs flag.
model.scope_statement: WM-XCT-036 covers the complete alias assertion: the two assertion endpoints and their declared subject plane; the single relation kind drawn from a governed, non-overlapping relation-kind register; the formal relation properties (directionality, symmetry, reflexivity, transitivity, invertibility) declared per kind; the ordinal semantic-strength rank and the inference-permission flag; the contextual and temporal scope in which the assertion holds; the asserting authority, justification category, evidence reference and confidence value; the lifecycle of the assertion and of its classification, including downgrade, upgrade, supersession and retirement; explicit negative (not-same) assertions distinguished from unknown, unassessed and absent; and the declarative conflict, cycle and invalid-combination rules that make overclaiming detectable. External vocabularies such as OWL 2, SKOS, schema.org, DCMI Terms, IETF link relations and HL7 FHIR link types are carried as versioned alignment bindings, never as conformance claims. The model asserts and classifies; it does not resolve, match, merge, redirect, reason or adjudicate.
in_scope: Assertion endpoints with declared subject plane (identifier, record, real-world entity, name or label, representation, referent replacement)
A governed register of mutually exclusive relation kinds with normative definitions and discriminating tests
Per-kind declaration of directionality, symmetry, reflexivity, transitivity, invertibility, allowed endpoint types and contextual scope
Ordinal semantic-strength rank and an explicit inference-permission flag stated as declaration only
Versioned alignment bindings from local relation kinds to external vocabulary terms
Asserting authority, justification category, evidence reference and confidence value carried on each assertion
Explicit not-same assertions held separately from unknown, unassessed and absent states
Classification lifecycle: assertion, downgrade, upgrade, supersession, deprecation and retirement of relation kinds
Declarative invalid-combination, contradiction and cycle rules used to make misuse detectable
out_of_scope: Ownership, content, validity or lifecycle of the endpoint records themselves
Entity matching, record linkage, similarity scoring or candidate generation algorithms
Adjudication of evidence and the decision procedure that concludes two things are the same
Data merge, survivorship, golden-record construction or record consolidation
Execution of HTTP redirects, canonical link emission or any runtime resolution behaviour
Computation of transitive or equivalence closure, entailment, materialisation or any reasoning regime
Allocation, minting, formatting or validation of identifiers and identifier schemes
Naming, labelling, transliteration and multilingual label governance
Runtime enforcement of the declared rules and the audit-trail semantics of any enforcement engine
Access-control decision-making and the retention execution machinery of the adopting Dimension

boundary_notes.distinction: WM-XCT-036 may declare that a relation kind is bound to owl:sameAs and that inference is permitted, but the satisfaction conditions, entailment and any closure computation remain with the OWL 2 semantics and the executing reasoner. This model never materialises inferred equivalences.

boundary_notes.neighbor: SKOS concept schemes and thesaurus management
boundary_notes.distinction: SKOS mapping properties link concepts across concept schemes; this model records the binding and the strength but does not own concept schemes, concept definitions, hierarchy or the editorial process of a knowledge organization system.

Redirect status codes and the canonical link relation are runtime resolution behaviours of an origin server. This model may record that a referent-replacement assertion projects to a 301 or 308 response or to rel=canonical, but never executes, emits or validates the redirect.

boundary_notes.neighbor: Identifier issuance and identifier-scheme registries (parent WM-XCT-011)
boundary_notes.distinction: The authority that mints, formats and retires identifiers is the parent identity model. WM-XCT-036 consumes identifiers as endpoint references and asserts relations between them; it never allocates or reformats an identifier.

boundary_notes.neighbor: Entity resolution and master data management matching engines
boundary_notes.distinction: Match candidate generation, blocking, scoring and threshold tuning belong to a matching model. This model carries the resulting confidence value and justification category as declared assertion attributes and defines what strength that permits.

boundary_notes.neighbor: Record and description models such as clinical patient records
boundary_notes.distinction: Record-level link semantics such as FHIR Patient.link are a projection of the record-equivalence and referent-replacement planes. Record content, status and clinical semantics remain with the source record model.

The model carries a provenance reference and justification category on each assertion, but the audit trail, event log and tamper-evidence semantics belong to the adopting Dimension's provenance and audit models.

boundary_notes.neighbor: Naming, label and lexical variant models
boundary_notes.distinction: The name and label alias plane exists only so that a label variant is not mistaken for an equivalence between two subjects. Label governance, preferred-label selection and language tagging stay with the naming model.

sources.title: OWL 2 Web Ontology Language Structural Specification and Functional-Style Syntax (Second Edition)
sources.relevance: Defines the SameIndividual and DifferentIndividuals axioms and their RDF mapping to owl:sameAs and owl:differentFrom, grounding the strict-identity and explicit not-same relation kinds.

sources.title: OWL 2 Web Ontology Language Direct Semantics (Second Edition)
sources.relevance: Gives the satisfaction conditions for SameIndividual, where all named individuals map to the identical domain element, and for DifferentIndividuals, establishing that strict identity is an equality relation and therefore reflexive, symmetric and transitive.

sources.title: SKOS Simple Knowledge Organization System Reference
sources.relevance: Normative source for skos:exactMatch, skos:closeMatch, skos:mappingRelation and the label properties. S44 makes closeMatch, exactMatch and relatedMatch symmetric; S45 makes only exactMatch transitive; S42 makes exactMatch a sub-property of closeMatch; S46 makes exactMatch disjoint with broadMatch and relatedMatch.

sources.title: RDF 1.1 Concepts and Abstract Syntax
sources.relevance: States that IRIs have global scope so two appearances of an IRI denote the same resource, that the IRI owner determines the intended referent, and separates the IRI, the resource denoted and any retrieved representation.

sources.title: Architecture of the World Wide Web, Volume One
sources.relevance: Defines URI collision, where the same URI directly identifies different resources, and URI aliases, and gives the good-practice constraint that a URI owner should not associate arbitrarily different URIs with the same resource. Grounds the identifier-alias plane and the resource versus representation distinction.

sources.title: RFC 9110: HTTP Semantics
sources.relevance: Section 15.4 distinguishes permanent redirection (301, 308) from temporary redirection (302, 303, 307) and frames redirection as guidance on which URI to target for future requests, not as an assertion that two resources denote the same entity.

sources.title: RFC 6596: The Canonical Link Relation
sources.relevance: Defines rel=canonical as specifying the preferred IRI from a set of resources whose content is duplicative or a superset, an explicitly representation-level preference and not a referent-identity claim; it is also informational rather than standards-track.

sources.title: RFC 8288: Web Linking
sources.relevance: Establishes the four-part link model of context IRI, relation type, target IRI and target attributes, and states that relation types are directional and are either IANA-registered tokens or extension URIs. Grounds directionality and endpoint typing for representation-level relations.

sources.title: Link Relation Types registry
sources.relevance: Normative registry entries for canonical, alternate, duplicate, successor-version, predecessor-version and latest-version, showing that representation equivalence, version succession and preference are separately registered relations rather than a single sameness link.

sources.title: schema.org property: sameAs
sources.relevance: Defines sameAs as the URL of a reference web page that unambiguously indicates the item's identity, with expected type URL on domain Thing. Confirms that schema.org sameAs is a reference-page pointer, not an OWL identity axiom.

sources.title: DCMI Metadata Terms
sources.relevance: Defines dcterms:replaces and dcterms:isReplacedBy as a related resource supplanted, displaced or superseded by the described resource and the inverse, plus dcterms:identifier, grounding the referent-replacement plane and the distinction between replacement and equivalence.

sources.title: HL7 FHIR Release 5: Patient resource, including Patient.link
sources.relevance: Provides a production example of a record-equivalence taxonomy with four disjoint link types (replaced-by, replaces, refer, seealso) plus an active flag, demonstrating that record supersession and record cross-reference are distinct kinds and that neither equals real-world entity identity.

sources.title: A Simple Standard for Sharing Ontological Mappings (SSSOM)
sources.organization: Matentzoglu, Balhoff, Bello and colleagues, in Database (Oxford)
sources.relevance: Defines a mapping as subject_id, predicate_id and object_id with justification, confidence, subject and object type, cardinality and a predicate modifier that negates the predicate; argues that mappings lacking semantics and provenance metadata are unsafe to reuse.

sources.title: Wikidata Property P460: said to be the same as
sources.version_or_date: Live property page, state as accessed 2026-09-04
sources.relevance: A deployed, symmetric, deliberately hedged sameness property described as this item is said to be the same as that item though this may be uncertain or disputed, with sourcing-circumstance and determination-method qualifiers; the contrasting P1889 different from and P2888 exact match show a live three-way split between probable, negative and exact claims.

sources.title: When owl:sameAs Isn't the Same: An Analysis of Identity in Linked Data
sources.organization: Halpin, Hayes, McCusker, McGuinness and Thompson, ISWC 2010, Springer LNCS 6496
sources.version_or_date: International Semantic Web Conference 2010, LNCS volume 6496
sources.relevance: Secondary evidence of systematic owl:sameAs misuse in deployed Linked Data, of identity behaving as a scale rather than a binary, and of referentially opaque contexts where identity substitution is invalid. Used to discover omissions and competing interpretations, not to establish normative structure.

sources.title: OWL 2 Web Ontology Language Primer (Second Edition)
sources.relevance: States that OWL does not assume that different names denote different individuals, so difference must be asserted explicitly. Grounds the rule that absence of an alias assertion is not a not-same claim.

bundles.name: Relation Kind Taxonomy and Semantic Strength
bundles.description: The governed catalogue of mutually exclusive relation kinds, their formal logical properties, their ordinal semantic strength and inference permission, the subject plane each assertion operates on, and the versioned bindings that project each kind onto external vocabularies.
bundles.rationale: Deployed practice collapses many materially different claims into a single sameAs link, and primary sources disagree on what that link means: OWL 2 interprets sameAs as domain-element equality, SKOS deliberately separates exactMatch from owl:sameAs and withholds transitivity from closeMatch, schema.org sameAs is a reference-page URL, and HTTP redirection is a request-targeting instruction. A discriminating taxonomy with declared formal properties is the only way an agent can tell which claim is actually being made.

layers.name: Relation Kind Catalogue and External Bindings
layers.description: Defines the closed, governed set of relation kinds with non-overlapping normative definitions and discriminating tests, and the versioned crosswalk that binds each kind to external vocabulary terms as an alignment rather than a conformance claim.

findings.name: Governed register of mutually exclusive relation kinds
findings.description: WM-XCT-036 recognises nine relation kinds, each with a normative definition and a discriminating test that separates it from its nearest neighbour: identifier-alias, where two identifiers designate the same subject within a declared identifier system; historical-identifier, a former identifier superseded by a current one for the same subject; referent-replacement, where the source resource or record is supplanted by a replacement that may be a different subject after a merge; exact-semantic-match, where terms are interchangeable across a wide range of retrieval applications; close-match, where terms are interchangeable in some applications only; equivalent-in-context, where equivalence is asserted only inside a declared context and is void outside it; probable-entity-match, an evidence-weighted, non-asserted hypothesis that two records denote one entity; not-same-assertion, an explicit negative claim; and strict-identity, a formal claim that both endpoints denote one and the same individual. Exactly one kind is assigned per assertion. Register status, effective interval and successor are held per kind so that retirement of a kind is itself governed.

questions.text: Which relation kind in the register exactly matches the claim being made, and what is that kind's normative definition?
What discriminating test separates the selected relation kind from the adjacent kind that would otherwise be chosen?
answer_data: outcome of the test for this assertion

questions.text: Which role is authorised to add, amend or retire a relation kind in the register, and under which decision record?
Is exactly one relation kind carried on this assertion, and how is a multi-kind or blended claim rejected?
What is the register status of the relation kind, and if it is deprecated which successor kind replaces it?

data_elements.name: relation_kind_code
data_elements.description: Controlled code identifying exactly one relation kind from the governed register.

data_elements.name: kind_normative_definition
data_elements.description: The normative definition text of the relation kind as published in the register release in force.

data_elements.name: kind_discriminating_test
data_elements.description: Stated test that distinguishes this kind from its nearest neighbouring kinds, expressed so that a wrong assignment is detectable.

data_elements.name: kind_register_status
data_elements.description: Governed status of the relation kind: proposed, active, deprecated or withdrawn.

data_elements.name: kind_successor_code
data_elements.description: Relation kind that replaces a deprecated kind; absent while the kind is active.

artifacts.name: Relation Kind Register
artifacts.description: The published, versioned register of relation kinds carrying for each kind its code, normative definition, discriminating tests, register status, effective interval and successor. It is a declarative catalogue; nothing in it evaluates or enforces an assertion.
artifacts.identity_strategy: Register entries are keyed by the authoritative master-system relation-kind code issued by the register owner; a governed IRI is minted per kind within the adopting Dimension namespace; a ULID is assigned to a register release only where the master system issues no release identifier.

findings.name: Versioned alignment bindings to external vocabularies
findings.description: Each relation kind carries zero or more bindings to external terms, declared as alignments with an explicit comparability verdict (narrower, broader, equivalent-as-used or incomparable) and the dated edition the binding was read from. Representative bindings: strict-identity to owl:sameAs and SameIndividual; not-same-assertion to owl:differentFrom, DifferentIndividuals and the SSSOM predicate modifier that negates a predicate; exact-semantic-match to skos:exactMatch; close-match to skos:closeMatch; referent-replacement to dcterms:isReplacedBy, to HTTP 301 and 308 responses and to FHIR Patient.link replaced-by; identifier-alias to database secondary keys and to the registered alternate relation; representation preference to rel=canonical and the registered duplicate relation; probable-entity-match to Wikidata P460 with SSSOM confidence and justification. Bindings never assert conformance and never import the target's operational behaviour.

questions.text: Which external vocabulary term is this relation kind bound to, and is the binding recorded as an alignment rather than a conformance claim?
answer_data: external term IRI or registered token

questions.text: Is the external term narrower than, broader than, equivalent-as-used to, or incomparable with the local relation kind?
Which dated edition or release of the external vocabulary was the binding taken from, and when was it last reconfirmed?
What documented statement in the external specification supports the asserted binding strength?

data_elements.name: external_term_reference
data_elements.description: IRI or registered token of the external vocabulary term bound to the local relation kind.

data_elements.name: binding_comparability
data_elements.description: Verdict on how the external term compares with the local kind: narrower, broader, equivalent-as-used or incomparable.

data_elements.name: external_specification_edition
data_elements.description: Dated edition, version or registry snapshot of the external vocabulary from which the binding was read.

data_elements.name: binding_evidence_clause
data_elements.description: Reference to the specific clause, axiom or registry row in the external specification that supports the binding.

artifacts.name: Relation Kind Projection Crosswalk
artifacts.description: Published crosswalk from each local relation kind to external vocabulary terms, carrying the comparability verdict, the dated external edition, the supporting clause reference and recorded divergences. It documents alignment only and confers no conformance.
artifacts.identity_strategy: Each crosswalk row is keyed by the authoritative master-system pair of relation-kind code and external term identifier; a governed IRI is minted per crosswalk release; a ULID is used only when no master-system release identifier is available.

layers.name: Formal Relation Properties and Strength Control
layers.description: Declares, per relation kind, the logical properties that govern how the relation may be read, and the ordinal strength rank with an explicit inference-permission flag. All declarations are stated, never computed.

findings.name: Per-kind directionality, symmetry, reflexivity, transitivity and invertibility
findings.description: Every relation kind carries a property profile with four-valued property states (asserted, denied, not-asserted-by-source, not-applicable) so that silence in a source vocabulary is never recorded as a negative. Grounded profile examples: strict-identity is non-directional, symmetric, reflexive and transitive because the axiom is satisfied only when the named individuals map to the identical domain element; exact-semantic-match is symmetric and transitive under SKOS S44 and S45, with reflexivity not asserted by the source; close-match is symmetric under S44 but transitivity is deliberately withheld to prevent compound error, so it is recorded as denied rather than unstated; not-same-assertion is symmetric and irreflexive and is not transitive; referent-replacement and historical-identifier are directional and invertible through a declared inverse and are asserted as single hops, never as a chain closure; probable-entity-match is symmetric, consistent with the deployed symmetric said-to-be-the-same-as property, and its transitivity is denied.

questions.text: Is symmetry or reflexivity asserted for this relation kind by its source vocabulary, denied, or simply left unstated?
Is transitivity asserted, explicitly withheld, or unstated, and does the kind have a named inverse relation?
For a directional kind, which endpoint is the subject and which is the object, and what does reversing them change?
Is inference permitted from this relation kind, and which externally owned entailment regime would perform it?

data_elements.name: directionality
data_elements.description: Whether the relation kind is directional with distinct subject and object roles, or non-directional.

data_elements.name: symmetry_state
data_elements.description: Four-valued symmetry declaration: asserted, denied, not-asserted-by-source or not-applicable.

data_elements.name: reflexivity_state
data_elements.description: Four-valued reflexivity declaration; strict-identity is asserted reflexive, not-same-assertion is irreflexive, SKOS matches are not asserted by source.

data_elements.name: transitivity_state
data_elements.description: Four-valued transitivity declaration; close-match is denied, exact-semantic-match and strict-identity are asserted.

data_elements.name: inverse_relation_kind
data_elements.description: Relation kind that expresses the inverse reading of a directional kind, where one exists.

artifacts.name: Relation Property Matrix
artifacts.description: Matrix of relation kinds against directionality, symmetry, reflexivity, transitivity, invertibility, inference permission and the supporting source clause. It is a declaration surface only; it does not compute or materialise any closure.
artifacts.identity_strategy: Keyed by the authoritative master-system relation-kind code plus the identifier of the register release it was generated against; no separate serial number is issued, and a UUID is assigned only if that register release lacks a master-system identifier.

findings.name: Ordinal semantic strength and inference permission
findings.description: Each relation kind carries an ordinal strength rank on a single declared scale, from a non-asserted hypothesis (probable-entity-match), through scoped or retrieval-level interchangeability (close-match, equivalent-in-context, exact-semantic-match), through system-scoped designation (identifier-alias, historical-identifier, referent-replacement), to a maximal formal identity claim (strict-identity), with explicit negation (not-same-assertion) held on its own high-strength negative rank. Strength is a declared attribute of the kind, not a computed similarity score; a confidence value in the interval 0 to 1 may accompany an assertion but never upgrades its rank. The inference-permission flag states whether substitution or entailment is allowed at all, and any permitted inference is executed by an externally owned regime. Published analysis that identity behaves as a scale rather than a binary supports the ordinal treatment, while OWL semantics fix the maximal rank.

questions.text: What ordinal semantic-strength rank does this relation kind carry on the declared scale, and what is the scale's top rank?
Which downstream operations are prohibited at this strength rank without a higher-ranked assertion?
Under what recorded exception may a lower-strength assertion be consumed as if it were stronger, and who authorises that exception?
Does a confidence value accompany this assertion, and is it prevented from altering the declared strength rank?

data_elements.name: strength_rank
data_elements.description: Ordinal rank of the relation kind on the declared semantic-strength scale.

data_elements.name: inference_permitted
data_elements.description: Declared flag stating whether any inference or substitution may be drawn from the relation kind; execution belongs to an external regime.

data_elements.name: confidence_value
data_elements.description: Optional confidence in the interval 0 to 1 supplied by the asserting party, where 1 indicates full confidence.

data_elements.name: justification_category
data_elements.description: Controlled category describing how the assertion was justified, for example lexical, logical, human-curated or similarity-based.

findings.inline_only_rationale: Strength rank, inference permission, confidence and justification category are scalar attributes carried on the relation-kind register entry and on the individual assertion record. Publishing them as a separate artifact would duplicate the register and create a second place where the ordinal scale could drift. The scale definition itself is a short inline declaration held with the register release, and the reasoning regime that would act on the inference flag is owned outside this model, so there is nothing further to materialise here.

layers.name: Equivalence Planes and Endpoint Scope
layers.description: Separates the six planes on which an equivalence or replacement claim can be made and constrains which endpoint types and contextual scopes each relation kind admits.

findings.name: Six discriminated equivalence planes
findings.description: Every assertion declares exactly one plane. Identifier equivalence: two identifier tokens designate the same subject within a declared identifier system, which web architecture treats as a URI alias with acknowledged costs. Record equivalence: two records or descriptions concern the same subject, as with a record-level link between patient resources that concern the same actual individual. Real-world entity identity: the endpoints denote one and the same individual in a domain of discourse. Name or label alias: a lexical variant of a label, which is a property of one subject and never an equivalence between two subjects. Representation equivalence: two representations or serialisations of one resource, covered by registered relations such as alternate, duplicate and canonical, which RDF and web architecture keep separate from the resource denoted. Referent replacement: the referent, record or resource is supplanted or superseded rather than equated. Cross-plane assertions are rejected by default; a plane change requires a new assertion.

questions.text: On which of the six equivalence planes does this assertion operate?
What does each side of the assertion actually denote: an identifier token, a record, a resource, a label literal or a real-world entity?
Are the two endpoints on the same plane, and what is the rejection rule when they are not?
How is a name or label alias kept distinct from an equivalence between two distinct subjects?

data_elements.name: equivalence_plane
data_elements.description: Controlled code naming the plane on which the assertion operates: identifier, record, entity, label, representation or replacement.

data_elements.name: subject_endpoint_reference
data_elements.description: Reference to the subject endpoint, resolved through the owning identifier or record system and never minted by this model.

data_elements.name: object_endpoint_reference
data_elements.description: Reference to the object endpoint, resolved through the owning identifier or record system.

data_elements.name: endpoint_denotation_type
data_elements.description: Declared type of what each endpoint denotes, distinguishing identifier token, record, resource, label literal and real-world entity.

findings.inline_only_rationale: The plane declaration is a single coded attribute on each assertion plus a short definitional enumeration held with the relation-kind register release; it produces no separate deliverable. The endpoints it points at are records owned by other models, so materialising a plane artifact would either duplicate the register or begin to shadow endpoint records that this model must not own.

findings.name: Admissible endpoint types and contextual scope of an assertion
findings.description: Each relation kind declares which endpoint types it admits and the scope inside which the assertion holds. SKOS mapping properties are conventionally used between concepts in different concept schemes, so a semantic match asserted inside a single scheme is flagged. Identifier alias holds only within its declared identifier system or systems. Equivalent-in-context requires a named context such as jurisdiction, purpose, dataset or time window and is void outside it. Representation-level relations hold between a context IRI and a target IRI in the sense of the web-linking model. Strict identity admits only endpoints that denote individuals in a shared domain of discourse. Each assertion also declares a validity interval and what is recorded when an endpoint cannot be resolved, without this model attempting resolution.

questions.text: Which endpoint entity types are admissible for the selected relation kind, and does each endpoint satisfy them?
Over which validity interval and named context does this equivalence hold, and when does it lapse?
Which authority owns each endpoint, and is a cross-authority assertion permitted for this relation kind?
What is recorded when an endpoint reference cannot be resolved at the time the assertion is made?

data_elements.name: subject_type
data_elements.description: Declared type of the subject endpoint, for example ontology class, SKOS concept, named individual, record or identifier token.

data_elements.name: object_type
data_elements.description: Declared type of the object endpoint, drawn from the same controlled list as subject_type.

data_elements.name: context_scope_reference
data_elements.description: Named context, such as a jurisdiction, purpose, dataset or scheme pair, inside which an equivalent-in-context or otherwise scoped assertion holds.

data_elements.name: assertion_validity_interval
data_elements.description: Interval during which the assertion is claimed to hold, expressed as RFC 3339 start and end instants with seconds and explicit offset.

data_elements.name: endpoint_resolution_state
data_elements.description: Recorded state of each endpoint reference at assertion time: resolved, unresolvable or not-checked; this model records the state and does not perform resolution.

findings.inline_only_rationale: Endpoint typing and contextual scope are inline attributes of an individual assertion, and the admissible-type lists live as columns on the relation-kind register rather than as a separate deliverable. Producing an artifact here would require holding endpoint inventories or resolution results, which belong to the endpoint-owning and resolution models and are explicitly outside this model's boundary.

bundles.name: Applicability, Negation and Classification Integrity
bundles.description: The rules that make misuse of the taxonomy detectable: applicability tests with documented counterexamples, the separation of explicit not-same from unknown, unassessed and absent, and the declarative treatment of invalid combinations, cycles, contradictions and strength changes.
bundles.rationale: A taxonomy that cannot be shown to be misused is not falsifiable. Primary sources supply concrete counterexamples: OWL makes no unique-name assumption so absence proves nothing, SKOS withholds transitivity from closeMatch and declares exactMatch disjoint with broadMatch and relatedMatch, web architecture forbids one URI directly identifying different resources, HTTP redirection targets future requests rather than asserting identity, and canonical designates a preferred IRI for duplicated content. Deployed practice and published analysis show these are routinely overclaimed, so downgrade, negation and contradiction handling must be first-class.

layers.name: Applicability Rules and Counterexamples
layers.description: Defines when each relation kind may legitimately be used, the documented counterexamples that mark misuse, and the evidence threshold required before a high-strength kind may be asserted.

findings.name: Applicability tests, counterexamples and overclaiming detection
findings.description: Applicability is expressed as pass or fail tests bound to documented counterexamples so that misuse is detectable rather than merely discouraged. Standing counterexamples: asserting strict identity between a real-world entity and a web page describing it, which is a URI collision under web architecture and is exactly what schema.org sameAs points at when it names a reference page; asserting strict identity between two thesaurus concepts that are only interchangeable for retrieval, which SKOS separates from OWL identity; reading a permanent redirect as identity of the denoted things when the specification frames it as which URI to use for future requests; reading rel=canonical as sameness when it designates a preferred IRI for duplicative or superset content and is informational; chaining close-match transitively when SKOS withholds transitivity from it precisely to avoid compound error; attaching a probabilistic score to a strict-identity assertion. Each detected pattern names the lower-strength kind the assertion must be downgraded to. This model publishes the tests; running them and enforcing outcomes belongs to the adopting Dimension's validation and enforcement services.

questions.text: Which applicability test does this assertion fail, and which documented counterexample does it match?
What evidence must exist before a kind at this strength rank may be asserted at all?
Which overclaiming pattern is suspected, and which lower-strength relation kind is the correct replacement?
Which review step must complete before an assertion may be published at the top strength rank?

data_elements.name: applicability_test_reference
data_elements.description: Identifier of the published applicability test that governs use of a relation kind in a given plane and context.

data_elements.name: counterexample_reference
data_elements.description: Identifier of a documented counterexample demonstrating a misuse of a relation kind, together with its supporting source clause.

data_elements.name: evidence_reference
data_elements.description: Pointer to the evidence relied on for the assertion; the evidence itself and its adjudication are owned elsewhere.

data_elements.name: overclaim_pattern_code
data_elements.description: Code naming a recognised overclaiming pattern matched by an assertion, together with the recommended downgrade target.

artifacts.name: Applicability and Counterexample Test Set
artifacts.description: Published, versioned set of applicability tests, each paired with a documented counterexample, the source clause that grounds it and the recommended downgrade target. It is a declarative test catalogue: execution, verdict recording and any enforcement are performed by services outside this model.
artifacts.identity_strategy: Each test is keyed by the authoritative master-system test identifier issued by the register owner, expressed as a governed IRI within the adopting Dimension namespace; a ULID is assigned to a test-set release only where the master system issues no release identifier.

layers.name: Negation, Contradiction and Classification Change
layers.description: Holds explicit not-same assertions apart from unknown, unassessed and absent, and declares the invalid combinations, cycles, contradictory pairings and change-control obligations that apply when a classification is downgraded, upgraded or superseded.

findings.name: Explicit not-same held apart from unknown, unassessed and absent
findings.description: Four distinct states are recorded and never conflated. Explicit not-same is a positive assertion that the endpoints do not denote the same thing, projecting to owl:differentFrom and DifferentIndividuals, to the deployed different-from property, and to a negated mapping predicate in SSSOM. Unknown means the question was asked and no determination could be reached. Unassessed means the pair has never been examined. Absent means no record exists at all. Because OWL does not assume that different names denote different individuals, the absence of an alias assertion carries no negative content, and no consumer may read absence as a not-same claim. A not-same assertion carries its own justification category, evidence reference and validity interval, and is symmetric and irreflexive.

questions.text: Is this pair explicitly not-same, unknown, unassessed, or simply absent from the record set?
May the absence of an alias assertion be read as a not-same claim, and which open-world rule forbids it?
What evidence supports an explicit not-same assertion, as distinct from a failure to find a match?
How long is a not-same assertion retained after its endpoints are retired, and which policy owns that disposition?

data_elements.name: assertion_state
data_elements.description: Four-valued state distinguishing explicit not-same, unknown, unassessed and absent for a given endpoint pair and plane.

data_elements.name: predicate_negation_flag
data_elements.description: Flag negating the relation kind so that an assertion reads as not a match of this kind, mirroring the SSSOM predicate modifier.

data_elements.name: negative_evidence_class
data_elements.description: Class of evidence supporting an explicit negative claim, distinguished from mere absence of a positive match.

findings.inline_only_rationale: The negation and unknown-state distinction is a single coded attribute plus a negation flag on the assertion record, with supporting references pointing at evidence held by other models. There is no separately publishable deliverable, and creating one would either duplicate the assertion set or imply that this model stores the underlying evidence, which it does not.

findings.name: Invalid combinations, cycles, contradictions and strength change control
findings.description: Declarative integrity rules over sets of assertions. Contradiction: the same endpoint pair on the same plane and context may not carry both strict-identity and explicit not-same. Disjointness carried from SKOS: an exact match is disjoint with broad match and related match, so those combinations are invalid. Plane contradiction: strict identity on the entity plane conflicts with a referent-replacement assertion that treats the endpoints as distinct successive referents. Cycles: replacement and historical-identifier chains must be acyclic and must terminate in a current endpoint; a closed cycle is recorded as a defect for referral, not silently broken. Cardinality: strict identity on the entity plane implies a one-to-one pairing, while probable-entity-match may stand at many-to-many pending adjudication elsewhere. Change control: any change of relation kind is a new classification carrying the prior kind, the reason, the authorising role and effective and observation timestamps; upgrade to the top strength rank additionally requires an authority declaration and an evidence reference, and downgrade must preserve the superseded classification rather than overwrite it. Detection, adjudication and enforcement of these rules are performed by services outside this model.

questions.text: Which relation-kind combinations are declared mutually invalid for the same endpoint pair, plane and context?
What must be recorded when an assertion's relation kind is downgraded or upgraded?
Which effective interval and observation timestamp distinguish a superseded classification from the current one?
How is a replacement or historical-identifier chain handled when it closes on itself?
What event obliges a mandatory re-classification review of an existing assertion?

data_elements.name: invalid_combination_rule
data_elements.description: Declarative rule naming a pair or set of relation kinds that may not co-occur for the same endpoint pair, plane and context.

data_elements.name: prior_relation_kind
data_elements.description: Relation kind carried before a downgrade or upgrade, retained so that the classification history is reconstructible.

data_elements.name: classification_change_reason
data_elements.description: Controlled reason for a change of relation kind, such as new evidence, overclaim correction, external vocabulary revision or authority decision.

data_elements.name: mapping_cardinality
data_elements.description: Declared cardinality of the pairing, such as one-to-one, one-to-many, many-to-one or many-to-many.

data_elements.name: observation_timestamp
data_elements.description: RFC 3339 instant with seconds and explicit offset at which the classification was observed or ingested, recorded separately from the effective interval.

artifacts.name: Invalid Combination and Cycle Rule Catalogue
artifacts.description: Declarative catalogue of contradiction rules, disjointness rules carried from aligned vocabularies, cycle constraints on directed chains, cardinality expectations per relation kind and the mandatory content of a classification-change record. It states the rules; evaluating assertions against them, raising defects and enforcing outcomes are functions of services outside this model.
artifacts.identity_strategy: Each rule is keyed by the authoritative master-system rule identifier issued by the register owner and expressed as a governed IRI in the adopting Dimension namespace; a UUID is used only where the master system issues no identifier.

functions.name: Curate a relation kind in the register
functions.description: Add or amend a relation kind, its normative definition, discriminating tests and admissible planes, producing a new governed register release.
inputs: admissible plane and endpoint type list
outputs: change note against the previous release
preconditions: The proposing role is authorised by the register owner
No existing active kind already covers the proposed semantics
At least one primary source clause supports the proposed definition
effects: A new register release is published with the added or amended entry
Regeneration of the crosswalk and property matrix is requested
The prior register release is retained unchanged for reconstruction

functions.name: Assign exactly one relation kind and plane to an assertion
functions.description: Classify a candidate assertion by selecting one relation kind and one equivalence plane from the register in force, recording the justification category and, where supplied, a confidence value.
outputs: recorded strength rank and inference-permission flag
preconditions: Both endpoint references are supplied by their owning systems
The selected kind is active in the register release in force
The endpoints satisfy the kind's admissible endpoint types
effects: The assertion carries exactly one relation kind and one plane
Event time and observation time are recorded separately
No matching, merging or resolution is performed by this function

functions.name: Declare the formal property profile of a relation kind
functions.description: Record directionality, symmetry, reflexivity, transitivity, invertibility, inverse kind, strength rank and inference permission for a relation kind, using four-valued property states so that source silence is not recorded as denial.
inputs: source clause references for each property
outputs: list of properties left as not-asserted-by-source
preconditions: The relation kind exists and is active in the register
Each asserted property cites a resolvable source clause
effects: The property profile becomes the declared reading of the kind
Absent source support is recorded as not-asserted rather than denied
No closure, entailment or materialisation is computed

functions.name: Bind a relation kind to an external vocabulary term
functions.description: Record an alignment binding from a local relation kind to an external term, with a comparability verdict, the dated external edition and the supporting clause, explicitly without claiming conformance.
inputs: external term IRI or registered token
external specification edition or registry snapshot
outputs: recorded divergences between local and external semantics
preconditions: The external term is published in a citable, dated specification or registry
The comparability verdict is supported by a cited clause
effects: The binding is published as an alignment only
Conformance is not asserted and no target behaviour is imported
Divergences are recorded for consumers to inspect

functions.name: Record a downgrade or upgrade of an assertion's classification
functions.description: Register a change of relation kind on an existing assertion, preserving the prior classification, the reason, the authorising role and both effective and observation timestamps.
inputs: evidence reference where the change raises strength
preconditions: The proposed kind is active in the register release in force
An upgrade to the top strength rank carries an authority declaration and an evidence reference
The change is authorised by a role permitted to reclassify
effects: The superseded classification is retained rather than overwritten
Effective interval and observation timestamp are recorded separately
Adjudication of the underlying evidence remains with the owning model

functions.name: Declare a taxonomic conflict, contradiction or cycle
functions.description: Record that a set of assertions matches a declared invalid combination, contradiction or cycle rule, and refer it to the owning adjudication service.
inputs: assertion references in the conflicting set
matched invalid combination or cycle rule identifier
preconditions: The matched rule exists in the published rule catalogue
effects: The conflict is declared and made visible on the affected assertions
The declaration is referred for adjudication outside this model
No assertion is deleted, suppressed or enforced against by this function

functions.name: Retire a relation kind with successor mapping
functions.description: Deprecate or withdraw a relation kind, name its successor where one exists, and state the obligations for assertions still carrying the retired kind.
outputs: updated register entry with deprecated or withdrawn status
migration obligation statement for existing assertions
preconditions: The retirement is authorised by the register owner
The impact on existing assertions carrying the kind has been recorded
effects: The kind may no longer be assigned to new assertions after the effective timestamp
Existing assertions retain the retired kind until reclassified under change control
Historic register releases remain retrievable for reconstruction

composition.target: WM-XCT-011 parent identity and identifier model
composition.purpose: WM-XCT-036 consumes identifiers and identifier-scheme declarations from the parent model as endpoint references. Allocation, formatting, validation and retirement of identifiers stay with the parent; this model only asserts relations between identifiers already issued there.

composition.target: Adopting-Dimension host entity, record and concept models
composition.purpose: The alias assertion set is applied as a mixin to host models whose subjects need federated equivalence, without those models absorbing the relation taxonomy or the strength and negation machinery.

composition.target: OWL 2 Web Ontology Language identity axioms (owl:sameAs, SameIndividual, owl:differentFrom, DifferentIndividuals)
composition.purpose: Binds the strict-identity and explicit not-same kinds to OWL 2 axioms and carries the satisfaction conditions as the definition of the maximal strength rank. Entailment, closure and any reasoner behaviour remain owned by OWL 2 semantics and the executing reasoner.

composition.target: SKOS mapping and labelling properties (exactMatch, closeMatch, mappingRelation, altLabel)
composition.purpose: Binds exact-semantic-match, close-match and the name or label alias plane to SKOS terms, importing the symmetry, transitivity and disjointness declarations as documented properties. Concept schemes and thesaurus editing remain with SKOS-based models.
Records schema.org sameAs as a reference-page projection whose expected type is a URL, deliberately kept below the strict-identity rank so that it is not read as an OWL identity axiom.

composition.target: IETF HTTP semantics and web-linking relations (301, 308, rel=canonical, alternate, duplicate)
composition.purpose: Carries redirect and link-relation references as projections of referent replacement and representation equivalence. Redirect execution, link header emission and origin-server behaviour are not owned here.
Binds the referent-replacement kind and its inverse to DCMI supersession terms, keeping replacement distinct from equivalence.

Aligns justification category, confidence, subject and object type, cardinality and predicate negation with an established mapping-metadata vocabulary so that exchanged assertions remain interpretable. Mapping production and curation pipelines are not owned here.

composition.target: HL7 FHIR Patient.link record-level equivalence types
composition.purpose: Carries a deployed record-equivalence projection showing replaced-by, replaces, refer and seealso as distinct kinds. Record content, status semantics and clinical processing remain with the FHIR resource model.

composition.target: Wikidata identity properties P460, P1889 and P2888
composition.purpose: Provides deployed projections for probable-entity-match, explicit difference and exact match, including sourcing-circumstance and determination-method qualifiers. Wikidata editorial governance is not owned here.

composition.target: Adopting-Dimension entity resolution and matching model
composition.purpose: Supplies the candidate pairs, similarity scores and adjudication decisions that this model records as confidence and justification. Blocking, scoring, thresholding and match adjudication are not owned here.

composition.target: Adopting-Dimension validation, enforcement and audit services
composition.purpose: Executes the published applicability tests and conflict rules and holds the resulting verdicts and audit trail. This model declares the rules and receives conflict declarations; it does not evaluate, enforce or hold audit-trail semantics.

composition.target: Domain-specific alias profiles such as clinical, bibliographic or geospatial equivalence profiles
composition.purpose: Downstream profiles may constrain admissible relation kinds, planes, endpoint types and evidence thresholds for their subject area. They must not redefine the generic relation-kind semantics, strength scale, negation states or change-control machinery held here.

owner_package_requirements: Name a single register owner accountable for the relation-kind register, the property matrix, the crosswalk, the applicability test set and the conflict rule catalogue, with a published decision procedure for adding, amending and retiring kinds.

Declare which external models own endpoint records, identifier allocation, matching and adjudication, evidence storage, reasoning, redirect execution, enforcement and audit, and record the referral route to each.

Publish the assertion-authority policy: which roles may assert each relation kind, which additional authority declaration is required for the top strength rank, and which roles may reclassify or retire an assertion.
Set a reconfirmation cadence for external vocabulary bindings and a named role responsible for reviewing bindings when a bound specification or registry is revised.
dimension.namespace_guidance: Relation kind codes, plane codes, applicability test identifiers and conflict rule identifiers are minted in a namespace controlled by the adopting Dimension and are never reused after retirement. External vocabulary terms are always carried as full IRIs or registered tokens with their source registry, never rewritten into the local namespace. Endpoint references are carried verbatim in the form issued by their owning system, character for character, and are not normalised, re-cased or re-minted by this model.
registry_links: Vercy registry entry vr.wm-xct-036 as the governing record for this model and its status.
Parent registry entry for WM-XCT-011 as the source of identifier and identifier-scheme semantics.
IANA Link Relation Types registry as the authority for registered representation-level relations used in bindings.
External vocabulary registries cited in the crosswalk, each pinned to a dated edition or registry snapshot.

canonicalization_rules: An assertion's canonical form is the ordered tuple of subject endpoint reference, relation kind code, object endpoint reference, equivalence plane, context scope and effective interval; two assertions differing in any of these are distinct records, never duplicates.

For a symmetric relation kind, canonical ordering of endpoints is by the lexical order of the endpoint reference strings, so that a symmetric pair yields one canonical record; the symmetry declaration, not a second stored record, carries the reverse reading.

Endpoint references are compared character for character as issued; no case folding, whitespace trimming, scheme rewriting or percent-decoding is performed, because such normalisation would silently create or destroy identifier aliases.
Timestamps are canonicalised to RFC 3339 with seconds and an explicit offset or Z before comparison, with event time and observation time held in separate fields.
patch_rules: A change of relation kind, plane, strength rank or negation flag is never an in-place edit: it creates a new classification and retains the superseded one with its effective interval and change reason.
Correcting a typographical or reference error in an endpoint reference is a withdrawal of the assertion and a new assertion, because a changed endpoint is a different claim.

A register release is patched only by publishing a new release identifier; historic releases remain retrievable so that any past classification can be reconstructed against the definitions in force at the time.

Adding, amending or withdrawing an external vocabulary binding is a crosswalk-level patch that does not alter previously classified assertions; affected assertions are listed for review under change control.
compatibility_rules: Adding a new relation kind, plane code, applicability test or conflict rule is backward compatible; consumers must tolerate unknown codes by treating them as unrecognised rather than as a default sameness link.

Narrowing the definition of an existing kind, changing its strength rank, altering a declared formal property, or changing its inference-permission flag is a breaking change requiring a new major register release and a migration statement.
Retiring a kind requires either a successor mapping or an explicit statement that no successor exists; consumers must not silently substitute a stronger kind.
A consumer that cannot interpret the plane, strength rank or negation flag must not consume the assertion at all, rather than degrade it to an undifferentiated equivalence.

identity_priority: The authoritative master-system identifier issued by the owning register or source system for the relation kind, applicability test, conflict rule, crosswalk row or assertion.
A governed global identifier or IRI minted in the adopting Dimension namespace where no master-system identifier exists, expressed so that it resolves within the Dimension's registry.
A UUID or ULID assigned by the adopting Dimension as a last resort, recorded together with the reason no higher-priority identifier was available.
No date, version label, release name or ordinal position is ever used as an identifier; such values are attributes of a record and may change without changing the record's identity.
artifact_rules.timestamp_rule: All time values are recorded in RFC 3339 form with seconds and an explicit numeric offset or Z; local time without an offset is rejected. Event time, meaning the instant at which the asserted relation is claimed to take effect or to lapse, is recorded in fields separate from observation or ingestion time, meaning the instant at which the assertion, its classification or an endpoint resolution state was observed or received. Where the two differ, both are recorded and neither is derived from the other; where observation time is unknown it is left absent rather than defaulted to event time. Register releases, crosswalk reconfirmations and classification changes each carry their own observation timestamp with seconds and offset.
artifact_rules.serial_naming_rule: Serial artifacts such as the Relation Kind Register, the Projection Crosswalk and the Applicability Test Set are named by artifact name plus the master-system release identifier issued by the register owner, with a separately recorded release timestamp in RFC 3339 form; the release timestamp is metadata and is never used as the release name or identifier. Non-serial artifacts such as the Relation Property Matrix and the Conflict Rule Catalogue are named by artifact name plus the identifier of the register release they were generated against.
artifact_rules.integrity_rule: Every published artifact carries a content digest, the identifier of the register release it was generated from and the identifiers of the source editions cited in it. An assertion is internally consistent only if its relation kind is active in the cited register release, its plane and endpoint types are admissible for that kind, its strength rank matches the register entry, and it carries at most one relation kind. Any artifact whose digest, register release reference or source edition reference cannot be resolved is treated as unverified and must not be used to classify new assertions.

policies: Exactly one relation kind and one equivalence plane per assertion; blended, multi-kind or unlabelled sameness links are rejected at capture rather than downgraded silently.

Absence of an alias assertion is never evidence of non-identity; an explicit not-same claim must be asserted with its own justification and evidence reference, and unknown and unassessed are recorded distinctly from absence.
No inference, substitution, closure or materialisation is performed by this model; the inference-permission flag is a declaration consumed by an externally owned reasoning regime.

External vocabulary bindings are alignments with a dated edition and a comparability verdict; conformance to an external standard is never claimed without a cited clause, and recorded divergences are published alongside the binding.
Endpoint references are carried as issued by their owning systems and are never minted, normalised or reformatted here.
Any change of classification preserves the superseded classification; overwriting a relation kind in place is prohibited.

read: Reading a relation kind returns its definition, discriminating tests, formal property profile, strength rank, inference-permission flag, admissible planes and endpoint types, and register status, always resolved against a named register release.

Reading an assertion returns exactly one relation kind and plane together with strength rank, negation flag, justification category, optional confidence, context scope, validity interval, event time and observation time.
Reads must state the register release used; a read that cannot name the release in force is unresolved and must not be used to classify.
Reading a superseded classification is supported so that past assertions can be interpreted against the definitions in force when they were made.
create: Creating a relation kind requires an authorising decision record, a normative definition, at least one discriminating test against every neighbouring kind and at least one supporting primary source clause.

Creating an assertion requires both endpoint references with declared denotation types, exactly one active relation kind, one plane, a justification category, an observation timestamp and, for kinds above the scoped ranks, an evidence reference.
Creating a binding requires the external term identifier, the dated external edition, a comparability verdict and a supporting clause reference.
Creation is rejected where the endpoints fail the kind's admissible endpoint types or where the endpoints sit on different planes.
update: Updating a relation kind's definition, property profile, strength rank or inference-permission flag produces a new register release and a migration statement; prior releases are immutable.
Updating an assertion's classification is a downgrade or upgrade recorded through change control with prior kind, reason, authorising role and effective and observation timestamps.
Updating an endpoint reference is prohibited; the assertion is withdrawn and a new assertion is created.
Updating a binding requires a new comparability verdict and a fresh reconfirmation timestamp against the current external edition.
delete: Assertions and register entries are not hard-deleted by default. Withdrawal sets a terminal state and writes a tombstone carrying the record identifier, the terminal state, the withdrawal reason, the authorising role, and event and observation timestamps in RFC 3339 form with seconds and offset; the tombstone is retained so that a previously exchanged assertion can still be interpreted as withdrawn rather than silently vanishing.

Explicit not-same assertions and withdrawn high-strength assertions are retained for at least the retention period declared by the adopting Dimension, because their disappearance would allow a previously rejected identity claim to be re-asserted without trace.
Retirement of a relation kind never deletes assertions that carry it; those assertions remain readable against the historic register release until reclassified under change control.

Hard deletion, erasure and purge are outside this model's boundary: the retention schedule, legal-hold determination and erasure execution are owned by the adopting Dimension's retention and data-protection policy and by the systems that own the endpoint records. This model declares only the tombstone and minimum-retention requirements for its own assertion and register records, and refers deletion requests to those owners.

Where an endpoint record is erased by its owning system, the assertion is withdrawn with a reason indicating endpoint erasure and the endpoint reference is replaced by a non-resolving withdrawal marker in accordance with the owning policy; this model does not itself erase or propagate erasure.

roles.name: Relation register owner
responsibilities: Approve additions, amendments, deprecations and retirements of relation kinds and publish register releases.
Maintain the discriminating tests so that adjacent kinds remain separable.
Own the strength scale definition and any change to a kind's rank or inference-permission flag.

roles.name: Alignment steward
responsibilities: Maintain crosswalk bindings to external vocabularies with dated editions and comparability verdicts.
Reconfirm bindings when a bound specification or registry is revised and record divergences.
Reject bindings that would import a target model's operational behaviour or imply conformance without evidence.

roles.name: Assertion author
responsibilities: Select exactly one relation kind and plane for each assertion and record the justification category and evidence reference.
Record confidence supplied by an external matching process without letting it alter the declared strength rank.
Record event time and observation time separately and declare the endpoint resolution state.

roles.name: Classification reviewer
responsibilities: Review assertions proposed at the top strength rank and record the review outcome and timestamp.
Initiate downgrades where an overclaiming pattern is matched, preserving the superseded classification.
Declare taxonomic conflicts and cycles and refer them to the owning adjudication service.

roles.name: Boundary custodian
responsibilities: Check that no bundle, layer, finding or function acquires matching, merging, resolution, reasoning, enforcement or audit-trail semantics.
Maintain the out-of-scope and boundary-note entries and the referral routes to owning models.
Block downstream profiles that attempt to redefine generic taxonomy semantics rather than constrain them.

access.default_rule: Relation kind definitions, property profiles, strength ranks, crosswalks, applicability tests and conflict rules are readable to any agent authorised to consume the model, because a consumer that cannot read the semantics will default to an undifferentiated sameness link. Individual assertions inherit the access classification of the more restricted of their two endpoints, since an alias assertion between two records can disclose a linkage that neither endpoint discloses alone.
exceptions: Assertions whose endpoints denote natural persons, or whose linkage would reveal a protected association, are restricted to roles cleared by the adopting Dimension's data-protection policy even where both endpoints are individually readable.

Probable-entity-match assertions below the adopting Dimension's publication threshold are restricted to the matching and review roles until adjudicated, to prevent an unadjudicated hypothesis circulating as an equivalence.

Explicit not-same assertions may be readable where the corresponding positive assertion is restricted, because suppressing a negative claim risks a downstream system re-asserting the rejected identity.
Superseded classifications are readable to reviewers and boundary custodians even where the current classification is restricted, so that a downgrade can be examined by the owning audit service.
audit_requirements: Every register release, binding change, classification change, withdrawal and conflict declaration emits a record carrying the acting role, the reason and both event and observation timestamps, which is handed to the adopting Dimension's audit service; this model does not define audit-trail semantics or retain the trail.
Access to restricted assertions is logged by the adopting Dimension's access-control service; this model declares the classification rule only and neither evaluates nor enforces access decisions.
Any consumption of an assertion at a strength rank higher than its declared rank must be traceable to a recorded exception with an authorising role and validity interval.

required_fields: Boundary statement listing the owning models for matching, adjudication, reasoning, redirect execution, enforcement and audit
read_order: Read AGENTS.md first and resolve Name, Type, Specification URL, Storage type URL, Interface URL and Processes URL before any other access, regardless of whether the storage projection is a document store, a graph, a repository or a service interface.
Read the Specification URL to obtain the relation-kind register, plane codes, property matrix and strength scale, and note the register release identifier in force.

Read the Storage type URL and Interface URL to learn how assertions are projected and addressed, treating any JSON, YAML, Markdown, HTML, Git, MCP or MongoDB form as a projection rather than as the semantics.
Read the Processes URL for the classification, downgrade, upgrade, withdrawal and conflict-referral procedures and the roles authorised for each.
Read the boundary statement last and follow its referral routes before attempting any matching, merging, resolution, reasoning, enforcement or audit operation, none of which this model performs.

coverage.claim: This model gives a defensible, source-grounded taxonomy for federated identity equivalence: nine mutually exclusive relation kinds with discriminating tests, six discriminated equivalence planes, per-kind formal property declarations using four-valued states, an ordinal strength scale with an explicit inference-permission flag, versioned alignment bindings to OWL 2, SKOS, schema.org, DCMI Terms, IETF and IANA link relations, FHIR record links, SSSOM mapping metadata and deployed Wikidata properties, plus first-class negation, contradiction, cycle and change-control declarations. It is deliberately bounded: it asserts and classifies but does not match, adjudicate, merge, redirect, reason, enforce or audit. It is not a claim of universal completeness; the relation-kind set is the smallest set that keeps the cited primary semantics separable, and it is expected to be extended by the register owner as new counterexamples are documented.

checklist.notes: Endpoint denotation types, the six equivalence planes and the strict-identity kind grounded in OWL 2 satisfaction conditions separate identifier identity, record identity and real-world entity identity. Identifier minting is explicitly the parent model's.

Register status with successor mapping, assertion withdrawal with tombstone, and downgrade or upgrade change control that retains superseded classifications. Endpoint record lifecycle is out of scope.
Per-kind directionality, symmetry, reflexivity, transitivity and invertibility are declared with four-valued states, and inverse kinds are named. Closure is never computed.
Validity intervals for context-scoped equivalence, effective intervals for classifications, and event time recorded separately from observation or ingestion time in RFC 3339 with seconds and offset.
Asserting party, justification category, evidence reference, external specification edition and binding reconfirmation are carried. Evidence storage and adjudication belong to other models.
Endpoint owning authority is recorded per endpoint, register ownership and role responsibilities are defined, and referral routes to owning models are mandated in the boundary statement.
Applicability tests, documented counterexamples, invalid combination rules, cycle constraints and cardinality expectations are published as declarations. Execution and enforcement are external.

Assertions inherit the more restrictive endpoint classification because a linkage can disclose more than either endpoint alone; exceptions cover person linking, unadjudicated probable matches and negative assertions.

Tombstone and minimum-retention rules are declared for this model's own assertions and register entries; retention scheduling, legal hold and erasure execution are owned by the adopting Dimension's retention policy and the endpoint-owning systems.

Bindings to OWL 2, SKOS, schema.org, DCMI Terms, RFC 9110, RFC 6596, RFC 8288, the IANA registry, FHIR and SSSOM are carried as dated alignments with comparability verdicts and recorded divergences, never as conformance.
Ordinal strength rank plus an inference-permission flag, with a rule that a confidence value never upgrades a rank and that any permitted inference is executed by an externally owned regime.
Explicit not-same, unknown, unassessed and absent are four distinct recorded states, grounded in the absence of a unique-name assumption in OWL and in deployed negation mechanisms.

Cardinality codes are carried from SSSOM, but no cited primary source fixes cardinality semantics uniformly across all six planes, and the interaction between many-to-many probable matches and one-to-one strict identity is stated as a rule without primary support. Marked as a gap rather than presented as canonical.

known_omissions: No jurisdiction-specific legal constraints on linking natural-person records are modelled; the adopting Dimension must supply them through its data-protection policy.
Bitemporal reconstruction beyond effective interval plus observation time is not modelled; a full valid-time and transaction-time bitemporal model is left to a sibling model.
Confidence calibration is not defined: the model carries a value in the interval 0 to 1 and its justification category but does not standardise how scores from different matching engines compare.
Multilingual and script-variant label equivalence is only recognised as a plane; the naming model owns transliteration, language tagging and preferred-label selection.

Relation kinds for part-whole, version succession and broader or narrower mapping are deliberately excluded, since they are not sameness claims; consumers needing them should use the aligned SKOS hierarchical mappings or a version model.
Group-level or bulk equivalence between whole datasets or schemes is not modelled; only pairwise assertions between two endpoints are in scope.
conflicts: The token sameAs denotes materially different claims across sources: OWL 2 interprets it as identity of domain elements, while schema.org sameAs expects the URL of a reference web page that indicates the item's identity. Binding both to the same local kind would be an overclaim, so they are bound to different strength ranks.

SKOS makes exactMatch transitive and symmetric yet explicitly separates it from owl:sameAs; consumers that chain exactMatch and then read the chain as identity produce unsound conclusions, so the model records exactMatch transitivity as scheme-scoped and prohibits promotion to strict identity without a separate assertion.

RFC 6596 is Informational rather than standards-track and defines canonical as a preferred IRI for duplicative or superset content, whereas widespread practice reads rel=canonical as sameness of the referent. The model records the specification reading and flags the practice reading as a counterexample.

HTTP permanent redirection tells clients which URI to use for future requests; it does not assert that two resources denote the same entity, yet redirect chains are commonly harvested as identity links.

Web architecture advises against associating arbitrarily different URIs with the same resource, while Linked Data practice depends on cross-dataset aliasing; the model treats identifier alias as legitimate but scoped, rather than resolving the disagreement.

The published SSSOM article documents match_type while the maintained specification uses mapping_justification and adds a predicate modifier for negation; version drift between the peer-reviewed article and the living specification means every binding must pin an edition.
Wikidata's deployed said-to-be-the-same-as property is symmetric and hedged, which conflicts with the common assumption that any recorded sameness property licenses substitution.
regional_assumptions: Endpoint references are assumed to be resolvable within the adopting Dimension's federation; no assumption is made that they resolve on the public web.
No assumption is made that a national or sectoral identifier authority exists for any given subject; where none exists, the governed-IRI and UUID or ULID fallbacks in the identity priority apply.
Legal restrictions on cross-register linking of person records vary by jurisdiction and are treated as an adopting-Dimension input rather than as a modelled constraint.
Language and script handling for the name or label alias plane assumes the adopting Dimension's naming model supplies language tags; no default language is assumed.
adversarial_checks: Boundary sweep against every relation rationale: each bundle, layer, finding and function was re-read for target-owned concepts. Matching, adjudication, merge, redirect execution, entailment and closure, identifier minting, label governance, access decision-making, retention execution and audit-trail semantics were all moved to out_of_scope, boundary_notes or composition references. The conflict function declares and refers; it does not detect or enforce. The applicability test set is a catalogue, not an evaluator.

Collapse test: an adversary asked whether the nine kinds could be reduced to a single sameAs plus a confidence number. They cannot, because closeMatch is non-transitive while exactMatch is transitive, strict identity licenses substitution while a probable match does not, replacement is directional while equivalence is not, and explicit negation is a positive claim with its own evidence. Collapsing them loses information that the cited primary sources declare.

Overclaim test: each proposed binding was checked for a citable clause. schema.org sameAs was deliberately not bound to the strict-identity rank because its expected type is the URL of a reference page; rel=canonical was not bound to identity because it is defined as a preferred IRI for duplicated content; HTTP 301 and 308 were bound only to referent replacement because the specification frames permanence as future request targeting.

Silence test: every formal property was checked for whether the source asserts it, denies it, or is silent. SKOS asserts symmetry for closeMatch and exactMatch and transitivity only for exactMatch, and is silent on reflexivity; the model therefore records reflexivity as not-asserted-by-source rather than inventing a value. Recording silence as denial was rejected as unsupported.

Negation test: the assumption that a missing alias implies non-identity was tested against OWL's explicit absence of a unique-name assumption and rejected; four distinct states were introduced so that unknown and unassessed cannot be read as negative, and a not-same claim must carry its own evidence.

Artifact discipline test: each finding was checked against the exclusive representation rule. Findings whose content is a scalar attribute of an assertion or register row, namely strength and inference, plane discrimination, endpoint scope and negation states, were given a substantive inline rationale and no artifact, to avoid materialising duplicate registers or shadowing endpoint records owned elsewhere.

Cycle and contradiction test: replacement chains, historical-identifier chains and combinations such as strict identity co-occurring with explicit not-same were examined. Rules were declared for each, with referral to an external adjudication service, and the model was checked to ensure it does not attempt to break cycles or resolve contradictions itself.
